analysis.one_liner: Requires employers without retirement plans to automatically enroll workers in payroll-deduction IRAs they can opt out of.
analysis.headline: The Automatic IRA Act of 2017 died in committee with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers with more than 10 employees that don't offer a retirement plan would have to automatically deduct a percentage of each worker's pay and deposit it into an IRA, unless the worker opts out. Workers who don't act are defaulted in at 3% of pay, adjustable between 2% and 6%. Employers who fail to provide access would owe a $100 penalty per employee, while small employers get a startup tax credit. Workers could also choose a government 'retirement bond' with inflation protection instead of a private IRA.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half of private-sector workers whose jobs offer no retirement plan. Today they can open an IRA on their own, but very few do; this bill makes saving the default, using the same behavioral trick that has sharply raised participation in 401(k) plans. It especially helps lower-wage workers at small and mid-size businesses, who can save without any paperwork of their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at jobs with no retirement plan

how_it_helps.text: Employers with more than 10 employees that do not maintain a qualifying retirement plan must make an automatic IRA arrangement available to eligible employees, who keep the right to opt out or change their contribution rate.

Employees who do nothing are treated as electing to contribute 3% of pay, with Treasury allowed to set a rate between 2% and 6%, and employers must send payroll deposits to an IRA or a Treasury 'retirement bond' designed to protect against inflation.
Employers that fail to provide access owe a $100 excise tax per affected employee, with waivers for reasonable-cause failures and for failures fixed within 90 days.

Employers with no more than 100 employees get a tax credit of $25 per contributing employee (capped at 10 employees) plus $500 in the first year and $250 in the second, and the separate small-employer pension startup credit is increased.

The bill directs Treasury and Labor to issue guidance making it easier for small employers to use multiple-employer plans, which let several unrelated businesses share the cost of one retirement plan.

analysis.who_pays: Employers without retirement plans bear new payroll-administration work and, if they don't comply, a $100-per-employee penalty; small ones get offsetting tax credits. Asset-management firms gain a large new flow of mandated accounts and their fees, which the bill polices only by barring 'unreasonable additional fees' on small balances. Workers pay entirely out of their own paychecks — there is no employer matching contribution.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers without plans; savers pay the full cost

drawbacks.text: There is no employer match: every dollar saved comes out of the worker's paycheck, which can squeeze households that are already short on cash. The bill's own text quietly acknowledges this — it waives the usual 10% early-withdrawal penalty for the first 90 days after someone is auto-enrolled, a release valve for people enrolled who cannot afford it.

Unless the employee picks their own IRA provider, the employer can route everyone's contributions to a designated trustee, so default savers may land in accounts with fees that, while not 'unreasonable' under the bill, still compound against small balances for decades.

The bill preempts state laws that would 'directly or indirectly prohibit or restrict' a qualifying automatic IRA arrangement, which would limit the room states have to run their own stronger mandatory retirement-savings programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is well supported by evidence: automatic enrollment with opt-out produces far higher retirement savings rates than opt-in, and the opt-out right, the contribution-rate limits, the small-balance fee restriction, and the safe government-bond default blunt the worst risks. The real weakness is that it asks the workers least able to save to fund their own retirement with no employer match and only modest credits for small employers, and its federal preemption would restrict states that tried to mandate employer contributions. On balance a genuinely helpful bill with real design compromises.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Neal, a senior member of the House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on July 27, 2017.
No representative joined as a cosponsor, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that don't offer retirement plans never faced the mandate or the $100-per-employee penalty, and their payroll operations stayed untouched. Workers at those jobs gained nothing; financial firms never gained the new accounts; and the state retirement-savings programs the bill would have preempted remained intact.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; a single Democrat sponsored the bill, no Republicans joined, and neither chamber acted.

industries.industry: Retirement plan administrators and asset managers
industries.note: The bill would create millions of new payroll-deduction IRA accounts routed through private IRA providers, making them the default channel for retirement saving at plans-less employers — even while requiring low-cost defaults, fee disclosure, and a government retirement-bond alternative. More workers saving means more fee-paying accounts for the industry.

industries.industry: Employers without workplace retirement plans (small and mid-size businesses)
industries.note: They would take on new payroll-withholding duties and a $100-per-employee excise tax for noncompliance; employers with 10 or fewer employees, governments, and churches are exempt, and employers under 100 employees receive offsetting tax credits.

Several states have set up their own automatic retirement-savings mandates for uncovered employers; the bill's preemption clause supersedes state laws that prohibit or restrict qualifying federal arrangements, narrowing the states' role even as it takes up the same goal nationally.
